candidato.titulo: Two new studies point to advances in personalized lung cancer treatment
candidato.resumo: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in the United States, but for a growing number of patients, the outlook is improving. As Lung Cancer Awareness Month draws attention to the disease and advances in care, Marina Garassino, M.D., a thoracic oncologist at the University of Chicago Medicine, is helping push the field forward.

texto_fonte:
Two new studies point to advances in personalized lung cancer treatment
Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in the United States, but for a growing number of patients, the outlook is improving. As Lung Cancer Awareness Month draws attention to the disease and advances in care, Marina Garassino, M.D., a thoracic oncologist at the University of Chicago Medicine, is helping push the field forward.
She has coauthored two new studies focused on making lung cancer treatment more personalized and effective. Both were published.
One paper informs when some patients should receive different types of treatment, while the other uses artificial intelligence to determine which patients may benefit most from a promising new drug.
Immunotherapy before lung cancer surgery improves five-year outcomes
A new five-year analysis of the international KEYNOTE-671 clinical trial, published in Annals of Oncology, finds that some patients with early-stage, operable non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) may have better outcomes when they receive chemotherapy and immunotherapy before surgery rather than receiving chemotherapy alone.
"Doctors' and patients' first instinct is to cut the tumor out immediately, which is understandable," said Garassino, a member of the trial's steering committee and senior author of the paper. "But our research demonstrates that in some cases, taking the time for chemotherapy and immunotherapy can increase the number of patients who are cured and improve overall survival with fewer recurrences."
The trial enrolled nearly 800 patients with resectable stage II or III NSCLC. Half received chemotherapy plus the immunotherapy drug pembrolizumab before surgery and continued pembrolizumab afterward. The other half received chemotherapy plus a placebo.
The five-year results show a significant difference between the groups. Nearly half (49.9%) of patients who received pembrolizumab were alive without their cancer returning or progressing five years later, nearly double the 26.5% of patients in the placebo group. Overall survival was also higher in the pembrolizumab group: 64.6%, compared with 53.6% in the placebo group.
Adding pembrolizumab did not worsen patients' reported quality of life. Side effects were consistent with what doctors would expect from the treatments.
The approach is now approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and has become the standard of care. Future studies will expand the patient population beyond those with clearly resectable tumors.
Garassino's message to patients with NSCLC: "Patience is worthwhile. Undergoing chemotherapy and immunotherapy before your surgery can change your life."
AI helps predict which lung cancer patients may benefit from a new drug
A second study, published in Nature Medicine with Garassino as first author, explores how artificial intelligence could help doctors identify which patients with NSCLC are most likely to benefit from a promising new treatment.
The drug, datopotamab deruxtecan (Dato-DXd), is designed to deliver powerful chemotherapy directly inside cancer cells. But not all eligible patients with lung cancer respond to it.
"We want to give the right drug to the right patients and spare anyone who is unlikely to benefit from possible side effects," Garassino said.
Dato-DXd targets a protein called TROP2 on the surface of cancer cells. However, about 90% of NSCLC tumors have TROP2, so the protein's presence or quantity alone isn't a reliable predictor of efficacy.
Garassino and her research collaborators suspected the answer lay in the protein's specific location inside the cell. They trained AI models to analyze digitized biopsy slides and calculate how TROP2 is distributed on the surface and inside thousands of cells.
"The protein concentration is visible in the cell cytoplasm, but the human eye is not able to give a quantitative score," Garassino said.
The analysis revealed that tumors with more TROP2 inside their cells were more likely to respond to Dato-DXd. Researchers suspect this pattern reflects cancer cells actively pulling the protein inward, potentially bringing the drug into the cells with it.
In a Phase III clinical trial, patients who tested positive for the AI-derived biomarker and received Dato-DXd lived a median of 17 months, compared with 10.8 months for those who tested negative.
Among patients who received standard chemotherapy instead, biomarker status did not affect survival. This suggests the test may help identify patients who are more likely to benefit specifically from Dato-DXd.
"It's an early example of how a good use of artificial intelligence and machine learning is able to improve precision medicine in clinical trials," Garassino said.
Publication details
H. Wakelee et al., Five-year outcomes of perioperative pembrolizumab for early-stage non-small-cell lung cancer from the randomized KEYNOTE-671 study, Annals of Oncology (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.annonc.2026.08.005
Marina C. Garassino et al., Normalized membrane ratio of TROP2 as a predictor of clinical outcomes with datopotamab deruxtecan in non-small-cell lung cancer, Nature Medicine (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41591-026-04716-9
Journal information: Annals of Oncology , Nature Medicine

candidato.titulo: Scientists pinpoint DNA copying 'traffic jams' impacting genome stability
candidato.resumo: Creating an accurate copy of the genome—the entire length of DNA in a cell—is the fundamental step before cells can divide, the basis on which all life sits. Errors in that duplication process—including replication pauses—lead to natural genetic changes that underpin evolution, but also give rise to diseases such as cancer.

texto_fonte:
Scientists pinpoint DNA copying 'traffic jams' impacting genome stability
Creating an accurate copy of the genome—the entire length of DNA in a cell—is the fundamental step before cells can divide, the basis on which all life sits. Errors in that duplication process—including replication pauses—lead to natural genetic changes that underpin evolution, but also give rise to diseases such as cancer.
However, identifying the frequency and impact of these events is inherently challenging due to their low frequency and delocalized nature across the genome.
Researchers in the Nieduszynski Group at Earlham Institute have now mapped locations in budding yeast where the copying machinery pauses, or stops altogether, in much greater detail. The paper "Single-molecule landscape of DNA replication pausing" is published in Nature Communications.
Head-on conflicts increase replication pauses
Using a single-molecule technology that labels newly made DNA with a chemical tag called BrdU, researchers could see individual replication events and determine where pauses occurred, which direction the replication machinery (replisome) was traveling, which DNA strand it was copying, roughly how long it paused, and whether replication resumed.
The study found that pauses are particularly prevalent in transcribed regions (around 20%–30% more problematic) and are particularly enhanced when transcription-replication conflicts are head-on.
While these conflicts have been observed before, previous techniques largely analyzed events at a population-scale level and therefore were unable to fully examine the scale of the problem or how frequently these events occurred.
Capturing rare events molecule by molecule
By working at the single-molecule level, the researchers can instead study individual replication events, as well as rarer events that would be difficult to detect using population-level approaches.
Dr. Sathish Thiyagarajan, postdoctoral researcher in the Nieduszynski Group, said, "We can see replication-pausing hotspots in much greater detail. More importantly, we now have a handle on how many replication events encounter problems. Because we can capture individual events, we can zoom in on particular genomic regions and see what's happening even when the event is relatively rare.
"So, if someone is interested in a particular gene and knows that problems in replication at that gene have downstream effects, this technique gives them a way to zoom in on that region and capture individual replication events."
The research builds on an earlier study by the Nieduszynski Group, which used the same single-molecule technology to map initiation sites—where the double-stranded helix teases apart to begin copying—finding that these initiation sites, like pausing, are dispersed across the genome, with around 80% of sites never identified before.
"Together with our earlier study, we can now track on a single DNA molecule where replication initiates, the obstacles it encounters, and the consequences for genome stability and gene regulation," adds Thiyagarajan.
Pause hotspots may reshape gene activity
The study found specific hotspots where parts of the copying machine come apart during a pause, which the researchers believe could act as a molecular switch, altering how that region of the genome is packaged and potentially having lasting effects on which genes are turned on or off in a cell.
At two particular sites, they found locations where the leading strand encountered an obstacle, while replication on the lagging strand continued.
Dr. Conrad Nieduszynski, group leader, said, "This work provides a powerful new way to identify difficult-to-replicate regions across genomes. These regions are likely to be hotspots for genetic and epigenetic change, with consequences that can range from microbial adaptation and biofilm formation to genome instability and disease in more complex organisms."
"One thing that we were pleased with was how well the technique could distinguish between replication on the leading and lagging strands. We knew the technique had the potential to distinguish between the two types of replication, but I thought we would need much more data to see meaningful differences. Instead, we saw many more leading-strand pauses than lagging-strand pauses at particular locations," said Thiyagarajan.
By making rare replication pauses easier to detect and quantify, the researchers hope to help scientists better understand how and why replication problems arise and how they may contribute to human genetic disorders.
Publication details
Sathish Thiyagarajan et al., Single-molecule landscape of DNA replication pausing, Nature Communications (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79296-w

candidato.titulo: NVIDIA reinstates Jensen Huang after 11-day absence
candidato.resumo: The NVIDIA board reversed its decision following discussions with Huang and senior U.S. government officials, amid growing pressure from the White House, investors and technology executives. The post NVIDIA reinstates Jensen Huang after 11-day absence appeared first on The Robot Report .

texto_fonte:
So much for robotics being in its post-Jensen Huang era. Just 11 days after his resignation amid allegations of personal misconduct and concerns about potential national security risks involving China, NVIDIA has reinstated Jensen Huang as president and CEO.
The company announced today that its board of directors unanimously voted to bring Huang back. Huang also returns to NVIDIA’s board, effective immediately.
NVIDIA said the board was satisfied with Huang’s candor and ability to lead the company. It also consulted with senior U.S. government officials before determining that his reinstatement poses no national security risk.
“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey Jones, NVIDIA’s board chair.
The decision marks a dramatic reversal for NVIDIA. During the company’s earnings call on Nov. 17, Jones explicitly ruled out bringing Huang back, saying the board had unanimously accepted his resignation and did not intend to reinstate him. Just six days later, the board unanimously voted to restore Huang to the position he had held since co-founding NVIDIA in 1993.
The reversal followed growing pressure from President Donald Trump, NVIDIA employees, investors and prominent technology executives. Trump publicly supported Huang’s potential return on Nov. 16, saying he would not object to his reinstatement. On Sunday, Nov. 22, Trump again urged NVIDIA’s board to bring Huang back.
Meanwhile, a “Stand With Jensen” petition attracted more than 200,000 signatures, including support from current and former NVIDIA employees, investors and technology leaders such as Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney.
NVIDIA also faced considerable financial uncertainty following Huang’s departure, with its market value falling sharply and questions emerging about who could replace an executive who had led the company for more than three decades.
It remains unclear precisely what persuaded the board to reverse course. NVIDIA did not identify which government officials were consulted or disclose what information they provided. The company also did not say whether the public campaign influenced its decision.
Colette Kress, who served as interim CEO following Huang’s resignation, will continue in her role as chief financial officer. Jones will remain board chair.
“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” Huang said. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.”
Huang also thanked NVIDIA’s board, employees, shareholders and his family for their support, adding, “I can’t wait to get back to work.”
National security investigation continues
Huang’s reinstatement does not end the scrutiny surrounding his departure. NVIDIA said an independent board committee will continue investigating reports that Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.
The committee has retained independent counsel, and Huang has committed to cooperating fully with the investigation. NVIDIA also recently established a National Security and Export Control Committee composed entirely of independent directors. The committee will oversee trade compliance and national security risks, with support from legal counsel and national security specialists.
The company did not provide a timeline for completing its internal investigation.
Huang’s return brings back robotics’ biggest champion
Huang’s return also restores one of the robotics industry’s most visible advocates to the helm of a company that has become increasingly important to robot development.
As The Robot Report previously examined, Huang has spent years promoting robotics and physical AI as major long-term opportunities. He has regularly featured robots in NVIDIA’s keynote presentations and helped bring greater attention to the industry’s potential.
Under his leadership, NVIDIA expanded its robotics portfolio with technologies including Isaac Sim, Isaac Lab, GR00T foundation models, Isaac ROS and Jetson computing platforms.
NVIDIA has also invested in and partnered with robotics developers, including humanoid companies, as it works to establish its technology as a foundation for robot training, simulation and deployment.

candidato.titulo: CNCF Research Shows Virtual Machines Remain Central as AI Workloads Evolve
candidato.resumo: New research from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) and Linux Foundation Research finds that VMs host an average of 53% of production applications, while emerging AI and agentic workloads are creating additional demand for virtualisation, particularly where stronger execution isolation is required. By Craig Risi

texto_fonte:
Virtual machines (VMs) continue to account for a substantial share of cloud-native production infrastructure, despite the widespread adoption of containers and Kubernetes. New research from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) and Linux Foundation Research finds that VMs host an average of 53% of production applications, while emerging AI and agentic workloads are creating additional demand for virtualisation, particularly where stronger execution isolation is required.
The report surveyed 492 cloud-native practitioners and technology leaders in September 2026. Among organisations expanding their VM footprint, 34% identified AI and agentic workloads as a contributing factor. The findings suggest that rather than replacing virtual machines with containers, organisations are increasingly combining the two to accommodate different application and security requirements.
The research challenges the assumption that cloud-native adoption necessarily means moving away from virtual machines. While containers provide portability and efficient application packaging, VMs continue to offer isolation and support for workloads that depend on dedicated operating systems or established virtualisation environments.
The survey found that 51% of respondents run at least half of their production applications on VMs. This rises to an average of 64% in organisations with more than 10,000 employees, compared with 45% among organisations with fewer than 500 employees.
Furthermore, 71% of respondents who provided both current and expected workload figures anticipate their VM share remaining within the same range over the next year. This points towards continued coexistence rather than a wholesale migration to one deployment model.
One of the more significant findings concerns the relationship between AI adoption and infrastructure security.
AI agents increasingly generate and execute code, interact with tools, and access external systems. This creates new risks when generated code is executed in environments containing sensitive data or shared infrastructure.
Virtual machines offer a stronger isolation boundary than conventional containers, which share the host operating system kernel. The report identifies hardware-level VM isolation, containers running inside VMs, and MicroVM sandboxing as approaches organisations are using to contain AI workloads.
Among organisations expanding their VM footprint, 47% cited security and isolation as a contributing factor, while 34% specifically identified AI and agentic workloads.
The survey also points to growing interest in stronger isolation technologies. MicroVM sandboxing adoption is expected to increase from 20% current use to 30% planned use, while confidential computing is expected to grow from 12% to 26%. These figures represent reported intentions rather than confirmed deployments.
Some 61% of respondents described their VM and container administration teams as collaborative or fully integrated, suggesting that managing different workload types is increasingly becoming a shared platform engineering responsibility.
Kubernetes is also beginning to play a role in virtual machine management. Among respondents using VMs, 8% reported using KubeVirt, the CNCF project that allows virtual machines to be managed through Kubernetes resources and APIs.
This brings VM lifecycle management into existing Kubernetes operational practices without requiring applications to abandon their virtualised environments.
The findings reinforce a shift in how cloud-native infrastructure is evolving. Kubernetes and containers remain important, but they are not necessarily the right execution model for every workload.
Technologies such as KubeVirt and Kata Containers show how virtualisation can integrate with container orchestration, while MicroVMs provide lightweight environments to isolate short-lived or potentially untrusted workloads.
For platform engineering teams, the research highlights the need to accommodate different execution environments without fragmenting operational practices. AI adds another dimension, making isolation, resource utilisation and workload security increasingly important infrastructure considerations.
The survey was sponsored by CNCF and Broadcom, and its results should be read as reported industry perspectives rather than a complete census of cloud-native deployments. Nevertheless, its findings provide a useful indication of where infrastructure priorities are moving.

candidato.titulo: Jensen Huang returns to applause from employees at Nvidia HQ
candidato.resumo: Jensen Huang returned to the office after being reinstated to CEO to cheers, according to videos spread on social media.

texto_fonte:
Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia on Monday after being reinstated as chief executive by the board. Videos on social media show the executive in a wool fleece, rather than his trademark leather jacket, with multiple floors' worth of office workers cheering him on.
Huang's remarks weren't shared alongside these videos, and words he did say aren't audible in the videos. But his words have leaked out to reporters and were posted on social media.
Bloomberg's Ed Ludlow posted on X that Huang thanked staff for a second chance, called today his "first day of work," and joked that the IT department needs to give him a new computer, which he hopes is RTX Spark-based.
"I am gonna be a better CEO the second time around," Huang reportedly promised.
The videos of cheering employees make it look like Huang came home to a hero's welcome, but not everyone seems happy. One anonymous engineer told Yahoo Finance that "This is the worst outcome. We already paid the price of his departure but are still saddled with working for a jerk."
Huang's return to power less than two weeks after his resignation came as a surprise, despite wide support from the tech community, an online petition, and some vocal Nvidia engineers. The announcement that Huang had been reinstated states that Nvidia's board "received input from senior levels of the United States government," with President Donald Trump praising the decision.
Huang will have plenty to contend with back in the corner office, including investigations from both the board and the SEC, as well as congressional inquiries into his relationship with Alice Huang, who reportedly was in regular contact with Chinese security services during her relationship with the Nvidia executive.
Nvidia's stock has increased more than 32% since the announcement of Huang's reinstatement.

candidato.titulo: Amateur Astronomer? Be a Kilonova Catcher!
candidato.resumo: Neutron stars are the ultra-dense, city-sized leftovers of dead stars. When they collide, they can release a brief flash of light called a kilonova. These immensely powerful events forge much of the universe’s gold, platinum and other heavy elements. texto_fonte:
Neutron stars are the ultra-dense, city-sized leftovers of dead stars. When they collide, they can release a brief flash of light called a kilonova. These immensely powerful events forge much of the universe’s gold, platinum and other heavy elements. Since a kilonova fades within days, astronomers have to find it fast, and no single observatory can watch the whole sky. But if you have a telescope with a camera, or access to one, you can help find and follow these cosmic fireworks as a part of NASA’s Kilonova Catcher project!
Kilonova Catcher connects amateur astronomers around the world into a rapid-response network. When gravitational wave detectors or space telescopes send out an alert, volunteers point their own telescopes at the sky to help find and track the fading light. The network also follows up on gamma-ray bursts, the most powerful explosions in the universe, and catches other short-lived cosmic events whenever the opportunity arises.
The Kilonova Catcher network has more than 150 registered members on several continents. Volunteers work side by side with professional astronomers and observatories. They have already contributed to more than 64 official reports shared through NASA’s General Coordinates Network, the system scientists use to share discoveries in real time. Volunteers’ observations have been credited for their contributions by being named authors in peer-reviewed scientific research papers. Kilonova Catcher volunteers also joined NASA’s lunar Impact Flash! project campaign during the Artemis II mission, recording the tiny flashes of light made when meteoroids strike the Moon. The network is getting ready to help follow up thousands of new alerts from NASA’s new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.
"Here at Kilonova Catcher, by chasing the light from gravitational-wave events, we’re seeing how a single collision reaches across the universe,” said Cristina Andrade, Kilonova Catcher head of operations at the Minnesota Institute for Astrophysics. “The observatories that make this possible will produce an unprecedented amount of data. We need more human minds, more people with their eyes on the sky and on the data, both literally and figuratively. And more importantly, we need more people to realize they are capable of great feats of science, regardless of their background."
The Kilonova Catcher project is co-led by Andrade and Principal Investigator Dr. Damien Turpin, a researcher at the French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission (CEA). Damien said, “I am inspired by the expertise and drive of our amateur astronomers. They are always digging for more information and pushing the limits of their understanding. This science could not be done without their contributions.”
To register and become a Kilonova Catcher, visit https://kilonovacatcher.in2p3.fr/ or send an email to kilonovacatcher@gmail.com. Anyone who has access to a telescope with a camera can take part!

candidato.titulo: Quantum Art Appoints Mark Solomon and Tal Inbar to Business Development Roles
candidato.resumo: Insider Brief PRESS RELEASE — Quantum Art, a developer of full-stack, fault tolerant quantum computers based on trapped-ion qubits and a proprietary, dynamically reconfigurable multi-core architecture, today announced two additions to its leadership team: Mark Solomon has joined as Head of U.S. Strategic Growth and Business Development, and Tal Inbar has joined as Senior Vice […]

texto_fonte:
Insider Brief
- Quantum Art has appointed Mark Solomon as Head of U.S. Strategic Growth and Business Development and Tal Inbar as Senior Vice President of Business Development.
- Solomon will lead U.S. commercial development, focusing on government agencies, national laboratories, research institutions and enterprise partnerships.
- Inbar will oversee business development outside the United States, focusing on international partnerships, market expansion and commercial strategy.
PRESS RELEASE — Quantum Art, a developer of full-stack, fault tolerant quantum computers based on trapped-ion qubits and a proprietary, dynamically reconfigurable multi-core architecture, today announced two additions to its leadership team: Mark Solomon has joined as Head of U.S. Strategic Growth and Business Development, and Tal Inbar has joined as Senior Vice President of Business Development, leading efforts outside of the United States.
Mark Solomon Named Head of U.S. Strategic Growth and Business Development
Mr. Solomon brings more than 35 years of experience in engineering, product management, strategic business development, technology commercialization, and market development. Most recently, he served as Vice President of Worldwide Sales at IonQ, where he played a key role in developing the company’s relationships and strategic engagement with the U.S. Federal Government. He joined IonQ as Director of Quantum Sales before advancing to Vice President. Mr. Solomon also represented IonQ at prominent industry forums, including Q2B and a Quantum Industry Coalition briefing in Washington, D.C.
Prior to IonQ, Mr. Solomon spent 35 years at IBM in various engineering, product management, and business development leadership roles. His experience included managing strategic research alliances, developing industry partnerships, and overseeing intellectual property licensing initiatives for IBM Research. Throughout his tenure, he received multiple IBM corporate awards for his contributions.
In his new role at Quantum Art, Mr. Solomon will lead the company’s U.S. strategic business development initiatives, focusing on expanding its market presence, cultivating high-value partnerships, and identifying opportunities to accelerate the adoption and commercialization of Quantum Art’s technology. Drawing on his 12+ years of experience working with quantum technologies and the quantum ecosystem, he will spearhead engagement with government agencies, national laboratories, research institutions, and enterprise organizations, building strategic relationships and developing new pathways for collaboration, innovation, and long-term growth.
“I’ve spent most of my career helping emerging technologies move from the lab into real-world applications through strategic partnerships and collaboration. What immediately stood out to me about Quantum Art is how far the team has already advanced its technology and its potential to transform the industry. I’m excited to work alongside this incredibly talented team to build meaningful partnerships, expand the ecosystem, and create new opportunities to bring this revolutionary technology to organizations across the U.S.,” said Mark Solomon, Head of U.S. Strategic Growth and Business Development at Quantum Art.
Tal Inbar Named SVP of Business Development
Tal Inbar brings more than 25 years of executive experience in business development, corporate strategy, M&A, and international business growth across the cybersecurity, telecommunications, and enterprise technology sectors. Most recently, she served as VP of Business Development & Strategic Alliances at quantum key distribution and quantum networking company HEQA Security, where she led global business development, sales, and strategic partnerships, driving significant revenue growth and international market expansion. Prior to that, she served as SVP of Business Development & Operations and a member of the top management team at NSO Group, where she played a key role in scaling the company’s business. During her tenure, she led global strategic partnerships and corporate development initiatives, including M&A transactions exceeding $100 million, joint ventures, and international commercial agreements. Earlier in her career, she held business development leadership positions at InfoGin and other technology companies and began her career as a corporate and M&A lawyer. She holds an Executive MBA with honors from Bar-Ilan University and an LL.B. from Tel Aviv University.
In her new role as Senior Vice President of Business Development at Quantum Art, Ms. Inbar will lead the company’s global business development and commercial strategy outside of the United States, focusing on expanding its international presence, establishing strategic partnerships, developing new markets, and creating business opportunities to accelerate the commercialization and adoption of Quantum Art’s quantum computing technology.
“Throughout my career, I’ve been drawn to transformative technologies and the opportunities they create. When I entered the quantum space, I quickly fell in love with the technology, its possibilities, and the incredible potential it holds to reshape industries. What excites me about Quantum Art is the opportunity to help turn that potential into reality, building partnerships, opening new markets, and creating the commercial foundations for long-term growth. I’m thrilled to be joining this team at such a pivotal moment in the evolution of quantum computing,” said Tal Inbar, Senior Vice President of Business Development at Quantum Art.
“Quantum Art is moving from technical milestones to commercial scale, and that transition is being driven by leaders whom buyers and partners already trust. Mark Solomon has spent his career bringing quantum technology to U.S. federal customers, and Tal Inbar has led global partnerships in quantum security. Together with our teams, they will put our trapped-ion systems in the hands of more customers around the world,” said Tal David, Co-Founder and CEO of Quantum Art.

candidato.titulo: Jensen is back: Nvidia board reinstates Huang as CEO
candidato.resumo: The move marks a sharp reversal by the board. Chair Harvey C. Jones said last week that the company had no plans to reinstate Huang as CEO, a statement that came after Huang said he would be "honored" to return if the board wanted him back. Read Entire Article

texto_fonte:
Winners & losers: Nvidia's board has unanimously reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as the company's president, CEO, and board director. The reappointment comes 11 days after Huang resigned following revelations of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a Singapore-based businesswoman whom US intelligence suspects of being a Chinese spy.
The move marks a sharp reversal by the board. Chair Harvey C. Jones said last week that the company had no plans to reinstate Huang as CEO, a statement that came after Huang said he would be "honored" to return if the board wanted him back.
 – WallStreetBets (@wallstreetbets) November 23, 2026
In an official statement, Nvidia said the decision followed input from senior US officials, who reportedly confirmed that his return posed no national security risk. The company said the board was confident in Huang's ability to lead, and that his reinstatement "is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers."
 – Trung Phan (@TrungTPhan) November 23, 2026
Nvidia said its investigation into the incident is continuing and that Huang's reappointment will not affect the process. "Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it," the company said, adding that it will continue to cooperate with ongoing government investigations and inquiries.
Nvidia's statement did not name any US official or elected politician, but the decision came a day after President Trump called for Huang's return. Trump posted on Truth Social that he hopes the Nvidia board will rehire Jensen Huang. "It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A.," he added.
In a statement following the announcement, Huang said he was honored to return to Nvidia and was taking on the responsibility "with the greatest humility and renewed commitment." He also thanked the board for believing in him and reinstating him as the company's president and chief executive.
Nvidia shares, which had slumped almost 50% from their October peak, surged 29% on news of Huang's reinstatement. The stock was trading up nearly 34% this morning from last Friday's 52-week low of $124.50. It's still trading about 31% below its all-time high of $243.37 from October 2026.
 – Morning Brew ☕️ (@MorningBrew) November 23, 2026
Huang resigned from Nvidia in disgrace days after The New York Times reported that he was "socializing" with Alice Huang, who US intelligence officials suspected of spying for Beijing. The relationship was subsequently confirmed as romantic by Financial Times before reports of at least two more affairs with Nvidia employees became public.

candidato.titulo: Agentic system personalizes physical controls to help users “DJ their art”
candidato.resumo: “TangiMap” uses an AI agent to reprogram how buttons, knobs, and sliders are used, helping users do things like edit photos and perform music in a more dynamic, tactile way.

texto_fonte:
In 2017, Apple removed the home button from its iPhones. Users lost a convenient, tangible control — part of a larger shift to digital buttons, knobs, and sliders we also see in cars (like with radio presets and air conditioning) and kitchens (see smart fridges).
We can’t leave physical controls behind entirely, though. They tend to be more convenient and efficient — think of how you can use a physical gaming controller without looking at it — and, at times, more precise, like when you use a dial to get the volume just right. But tangible controls are typically preprogrammed to do a specific thing, minimizing their usefulness.
A new system called “TangiMap,” co-developed by an MIT graduate student and researcher at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL), helps bring tangible control back to your software. The system personalizes the physical controls on everyday devices by mapping digital widgets onto tangible inputs, turning things like editing photos, animation, performing music, and creating 3D models into more dynamic and tactile experiences. Just as a DJ’s pads switch between triggering cues, loops, and samples, TangiMap gives a device’s controls entirely new roles.
But how, exactly? TangiMap relies on an AI agent, or semi-autonomous programs that “think” and complete well-defined tasks, to find and act on context about the software you’re using, your tendencies, and the device used to control that program. To gather the required context, the agent can draw on sources such as the program’s API (the rules that let programs talk to each other), an MCP server (a standard that connects AI agents to apps), or a screenshot interpreted by a vision-language model. Then, the agent uses a large language model to put all the info it's gathered into a file before mapping specific digital functions to physical controls.
“TangiMap builds on our broader vision of reprogramming common objects to be more dynamic,” says Yunyi Zhu ’20, MEng ’21, a doctoral student in the MIT Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and a CSAIL researcher whose advisor is MIT Associate Professor Stefanie Mueller. “Here, AI agents help us adapt physical controls to whatever we’re working on. We want to bring back physical controls so we can interact with our devices eyes-free, the way you adjust a car’s volume without looking away from the road. Physical controls also let you adjust several settings at once, like tweaking brightness and contrast together when editing an image, which is hard to do on a screen.”
The system helped the researchers turn a standard mixer into a photo-editing controller. That way, they could adjust color in Adobe Lightroom, with a complementary visualization of those controls displayed on their screen. The team did the same with sound-mixing software, so that performers can adjust their music in real-time with their own inputs to knobs and faders.
The researchers also reprogrammed a simpler mixer to work with the 3D modeling program Blender. Their interface included an area where users can type in a prompt, and once the model was generated, users could adjust features like shininess on a mixer using physical controls. Within Adobe’s Character Animator software, TangiMap connected specific expressions and movements to buttons on a control pad so users could animate (or “puppeteer”) a cartoon character live.
Zhu and co-author Chang Xiao, an assistant professor at Boston University, presented their tool at the ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology earlier this month.
Zhu and Xiao created a custom user interface (UI) for each application. While that adds another layer of personalization to the creative process, the team is hoping to create a more streamlined system that helps the designer to generate the UI for their device by taking a picture.
The researchers are also considering the physical aspects of user interactions. They want to use more ergonomic devices and also ensure that TangiMap accounts for where users position their hands when doing different tasks. For example, users typically hold a mixer differently when they’re using it to make music than, say, when playing a video game. You may want controls mapped closer or further apart, depending on what you’re doing.
Zhu is hoping to do a user study to get more feedback about TangiMap, and whether this kind of “smart DJing” could indeed improve those experiences. But the dynamic reprogramming she ultimately envisions is even more ambitious.
“The same way our phones and computers generalize to a range of tasks, we want other objects to be more intelligent,” she says. “I would like to build physical items that use an AI agent as a brain to decide what to reprogram into. They could understand what to transform into, given a specific situation.”
A chemical jar, for instance, could tell you if it’s sealed correctly when asked, and when you want to see what it’s typically used for, the container would instead display that information. While that kind of versatility and interactivity is a ways off, more powerful agents and more intricate fabrication pipelines could bring everyday objects to life.
Their work was supported, in part, by Google’s Gemini Academic Program Award.

candidato.titulo: The mystery of sub-Neptunes – the planets we thought shouldn’t exist
candidato.resumo: Sub-Neptunes are the most abundant exoplanets, but are unlike anything in our solar system. We are finally gaining tantalising clues about what they are and how they came to be

texto_fonte:
For almost a decade, the Kepler Space Telescope trailed Earth’s orbit, watching out for flickers in the light of distant stars. In 2011, two years after its launch, the NASA mission found what it was looking for: the signature of a roughly Earth-sized planet dimming out a tiny sliver of light as it transited across the face of its star.
The identification of Kepler-10b, a planet almost 1.5 times the size of Earth that orbits a star around 600 light years away, was the first time we had spotted a rocky exoplanet – a world beyond our solar system. Since then, our rapidly expanding exoplanet catalogue has revealed plenty of surprises, but one above all: most planets in our galaxy aren’t like Earth. In fact, they are like nothing in our solar system at all.
Out of the now 6451 confirmed exoplanets, by far the most common type are the “sub-Neptunes”, planets between Earth and Neptune in size that old theories of planet formation based on our solar system didn’t predict. And there are lots of them – over 3000 at the last count. “You know how evolution, like, really likes making crabs? Planet formation seems to really like making sub-Neptunes,” says astrophysicist Matthew Nixon at Arizona State University.
Advertisement
But there is no sub-Neptune in our solar system, and that leaves researchers with a puzzle: what exactly are these mysterious planets? Now, aided by NASA’s orbiting high-tech thermal camera, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), they are coming into sharper focus. New discoveries are answering some questions, but raising many more about what sub-Neptunes look like, how they form – and whether they might even host life.
Exoplanetary science is still young. Astronomers spotted the first planet beyond our solar system, a gas giant circling a pulsar, in 1992. In 1995 came the first exoplanet around a sun-like star, a giant, close-orbiting “hot Jupiter” called 51 Pegasi b. But the hunt didn’t hit its high season until Kepler launched in 2009. It flew with just one instrument: a photometer that could precisely measure stars’ brightness and catch the telltale flickers of passing planets. By the time the mission ran out of fuel in 2018, it had discovered over half of all exoplanets we know today.
Back in those early days, our ideas of how planets formed were guided by a sample of one: our solar system. It is widely agreed that our sun formed from the gravitational collapse of the solar nebula, a giant, spinning cloud of hydrogen and helium gas, plus a sprinkling of heavier elements. Once the young sun ignited, a disc of material continued circling it that would give rise to the planets.
Looking at our solar system, scientists broadly concluded that what planets look like came down to where they formed within this nebular Frisbee. Closer to the sun, it is too hot for anything but rock and metals to solidify and clump together, meaning less material to sweep up into planets. So, the planets of the inner solar system – Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars – ended up small and rocky. Meanwhile, in longer orbits beyond the “snow line”, where compounds such as water, ammonia and methane freeze out and form ices, baby planetary cores could get bigger. These bigger cores had the gravitational heft to gobble up hydrogen and helium gas from the solar nebula. They formed the outer solar system’s two gas giants, Jupiter and Saturn, and its more distant “ice giants”, Uranus and Neptune.
Earth is the solar system’s largest rocky planet; Neptune, at around four times Earth’s diameter, is its smallest giant planet. The gap in size between the two seemed natural. Given how we thought planets form, worlds much bigger than Earth should be incredibly rare within the snow line. That, it turns out, isn’t true.
Exoplanet astronomers have found everything from alien gas titans that would dwarf Jupiter to planetary pebbles comparable to Mercury. But among confirmed exoplanets with a known radius, about half are sub-Neptunes, many of them hewing in warm orbits very close to their stars. “They’re really the ultimate mystery,” says exoplanet astronomer Eliza Kempton at the University of Chicago.
Kempton has been studying sub-Neptunes since before they were called sub-Neptunes. In 2010, even before Kepler found that first Earth-sized planet, she and her colleagues used the ground-based Very Large Telescope facility in Chile to observe the hazy atmosphere of a planet called GJ 1214 b some 48 light years away from Earth. With a radius 2.7 times that of Earth, but orbiting far closer to its star than Mercury does to the sun, that planet is now something of a poster child for the sub-Neptunes. But back then, it was a “super-Earth”.
“We just called everything a super-Earth,” says Kempton. “This was before we even knew that small planets bifurcate into, like, the ‘smaller’ class and the ‘bigger’ class.” That divide refers to a striking discovery made in 2017 that deepened the mystery of sub-Neptunes further still. When astronomers used Kepler data to chart the number of exoplanets of different sizes, it revealed two bumps. One was centred on planets with radii about 1.4 times Earth’s, and another on those of about 2.4 Earth radii. In between, there was a gap with relatively few planets. The sub-Neptunes appeared to be not just one population of planets, but two.
The discovery of this “radius valley” lent support to an idea that harsh radiation emitted from young stars, plus leftover heat from planet formation, blasts away the baby blankets of hydrogen and helium gas enveloping smaller planets. That leaves bare, rocky worlds that form the super-Earth peak. Bigger planets with more gravity, meanwhile, hold onto at least some hydrogen and helium. They end up as puffier, gas-cloaked worlds in the sub-Neptune peak.
In this picture, terrestrial planets like Earth might be the naked cores of erstwhile sub-Neptunes. “If you’re ultimately interested in more Earth-like worlds, sub-Neptunes represent a kind of arrested stage of development. These are the things that stop short of becoming something like Earth,” says planetary scientist Raymond Pierrehumbert at the University of Oxford. “I think of them almost like fossilised atmospheres.”
Unlike the ice giants of our solar system, sub-Neptunes close to their stars might form pretty dry – as “gas dwarfs” with no ice, just a rocky interior and a thick gas envelope made almost entirely of hydrogen and helium. But there are other possibilities. The discovery of hot Jupiters – gas giant planets in close orbits where they couldn’t possibly have formed – helped scientists realise that planets can migrate, something we now know probably happened in our solar system, too. Sub-Neptunes could be ice worlds that form beyond their planetary system’s snow line and wander inwards. In some simulations, this migration produces a radius valley: one that divides small, rocky planets from big, watery ones.
Since JWST’s launch in 2021, astronomers have been able to start differentiating between such scenarios. Its great infrared eye sees in wavelengths of light at which molecules such as water, ammonia, carbon dioxide and methane leave distinctive fingerprints on starlight passing through exoplanets’ upper atmospheres.
In at least one case, that of the hot sub-Neptune TOI-421 b, which orbits its sun-like star far closer than Mercury does our sun, JWST observations largely match what you would expect for a gas dwarf. But observations are revealing that sub-Neptunes are a diverse group (see “Five ways to make a sub-Neptune”, below). If some of them are worlds with abundant water, it would be a big deal for the search for life. “Where you can find water, you can find habitable conditions,” says astrophysicist Caroline Piaulet-Ghorayeb also at the University of Chicago. Finding sub-Neptune water worlds “would kind of change our thinking about habitability”, she says. Earth-sized planets are very hard to observe in detail with JWST, so bigger water worlds could be our best immediate hope for finding signs of life on an exoplanet.
The mere presence of water doesn’t make a habitable planet. Sub-Neptunes could be balls of exotic, high-pressure ice and “supercritical” fluids that are neither liquid nor gas – mini ice giants, not ocean worlds. And because hydrogen is a strong greenhouse gas, sub-Neptunes with hydrogen atmospheres can end up as boiling “steam worlds” with atmospheres rich in water vapour. JWST observations suggest that a watery sub-Neptune called GJ 9827 d is such a planet.
However, in the lead-up to JWST’s launch, astrophysicist Nikku Madhusudhan at the University of Cambridge and his colleagues showed that water worlds with thin hydrogen atmospheres could have liquid water on their surfaces (too thick an atmosphere, and the water boils). Madhusudhan later dubbed these planets “Hycean” worlds, a portmanteau of “hydrogen” and “ocean”. JWST observations have hinted that a sub-Neptune called K2-18 b orbiting a star some 125 light years from Earth might belong to this group. It sits in its star’s habitable zone, where it is theoretically cool enough for surface liquid water.
This plot thickened in 2023, when Madhusudhan’s team spotted what it interpreted as tentative evidence for dimethyl sulphide (DMS) in K2-18 b’s atmosphere. On Earth, DMS is made only by life – primarily plankton in the ocean. The team doubled down after follow-up JWST observations, but the result remains fiercely disputed. Nixon objects that the data isn’t enough to uniquely identify a molecule as complex as DMS. “A lot of other molecules, if you were to test them, you would also get a comparable result,” he says. Madhusudhan stands by the detection. He argues that researchers have historically accepted detections of more mundane gases like CO2 based on comparable evidence.
If there is DMS on K2-18 b, it is possible that an unknown chemical process might produce it, rather than alien microbes. Madhusudhan says he would “absolutely” be happy either way. “The discovery of a new chemical process in a planetary atmosphere? I mean, that’s a huge deal,” he says. “To me, that is as good as finding life.”
But even the identification of K2-18 b as a Hycean world is disputed. What scientists see in sub-Neptunes’ atmospheres depends in large part on what happens out of view, deep in the planets’ hot, high-pressure interiors. The mix of molecules JWST has spotted in K2-18 b’s atmosphere matches a planet with water oceans – but might also fit a gaseous mini-Neptune without a real surface, or a gas dwarf with a magma ocean simmering below its hydrogen envelope.
Earth once had a magma ocean, too. Rocky worlds go through an initial molten phase with a global magma ocean before they cool down and solidify. Some sub-Neptunes might trap enough primordial heat below blankets of gas and icy material that their magma oceans never freeze – with significant consequences. “Magma oceans are a chemical factory,” says Pierrehumbert. “Chemicals can get in there and react and do all sorts of stuff.” One reason to think K2-18 b is a watery world is the lack of ammonia in its atmosphere: ammonia dissolves in water. But it also dissolves in liquid rock. So ultimately, researchers need to learn more about K2-18 b’s atmosphere to pin down its composition.
Magma oceans do more than conceal compounds such as ammonia – they “fundamentally change the composition of the atmosphere”, says Kempton. Reactions between hydrogen and magma could even produce abundant water on planets that were born dry, without any water, she adds. This process might have produced some of Earth’s water back when it had a magma ocean.
Magma isn’t the only thing that might be smouldering deep within sub-Neptunes. A study led by Kempton’s University of Chicago colleague Jeehyun Yang recently found that sub-Neptunes could be a bit like combustion engines, burning carbon-rich compounds to produce soot. A layer of these planets might be, rather literally, on fire, says Yang. Clouds of black soot belched up from below would block out some molecular signals, perhaps explaining a pattern of muted molecular fingerprints in JWST data from several sub-Neptunes.
Some worlds might make soot; others might actually be made of it. Just as there is a snow line beyond which water is solid, there is a “soot line” around young stars where organic carbon molecules can start to form grains of black, tarry material. Sub-Neptunes are reviving an old idea that this could create “soot worlds”, says planetary scientist Zifan Lin at Washington University in St. Louis, Missouri. Lin and his colleague Sara Seager at the University of Toronto recently showed that soot worlds with cores of rock and metal, overlain by layers of diamond and graphite and with hydrogen-rich atmospheres, could match JWST observations of three sub-Neptunes, including K2-18 b.
So, gas dwarfs, water worlds, soot planets – what’s the answer? The boundaries might be fuzzier than they sound. Recent work by Piaulet-Ghorayeb and her colleagues has shown that some sub-Neptunes that appear dry could hide water deep in their interiors, where it is invisible to telescopes. And there could be sooty water worlds, sooty gas dwarfs and everything in between.
One lesson sub-Neptunes have already taught scientists is that planetary evolution, not just formation, determines what worlds are made of. Losing an atmosphere or reacting one with a magma ocean, say, shapes a planet just as profoundly as forming beyond or within the snow line. Nixon says he is working on finding ways to distinguish between water worlds that wandered inwards and sub-Neptunes that formed dry and later made their own water. To this end, he is observing a hot sub-Neptune called HD 86226 that is virtually guaranteed to have a magma ocean, eliminating some guesswork.
Ideally, scientists would eventually like to understand whether sub-Neptunes are all basically variations on the same planetary theme, or are many sub-groups with different histories. Observations so far have pinpointed only a few molecules in a handful of sub-Neptunes’ atmospheres. Surveys of more sub-Neptunes are under way, and these could help pick out different groups if they exist.
The more we learn about sub-Neptunes, the more they surprise us, making them one of the most exciting active frontiers in exoplanetary science. We still don’t know why our solar system lacks one of these abundant worlds, but they are the closest thing to a world like Earth that we can observe easily at present. Through them, we learn not only about the broader universe, but also about the forces that sculpt worlds like our own. “The sub-Neptunes give us that next stepping stone,” says Kempton. “We’re kind of marching our way towards the study of Earth-like worlds in the future.”

Rumores apontam que a desenvolvedora tenta negociar o licenciamento da propriedade intelectual por US$ 100 milhões. As informações foram divulgadas pelo The Ankler, que indica que nenhuma produtora adquiriu o projeto ainda. Porém, a iniciativa de levar a saga para Hollywood pode ser genuína, principalmente quando se veem tantas versões ganharem destaque. Vale lembrar que o Red Dead Redemption 2 (2018) é um sucesso estrondoso, com 85 milhões de jogadores — o 3º mais vendido da história . De acordo com o vazamento, ela busca opções nos cinemas e em séries televisivas. texto_fonte:
Rockstar negocia direitos de filme e série de Red Dead Redemption
Por Diego Corumba |
A Rockstar Games busca ativamente estúdios interessados em produzir uma adaptação de Red Dead Redemption — sua franquia realista de velho-oeste. Rumores apontam que a desenvolvedora tenta negociar o licenciamento da propriedade intelectual por US$ 100 milhões.
As informações foram divulgadas pelo The Ankler, que indica que nenhuma produtora adquiriu o projeto ainda. Porém, a iniciativa de levar a saga para Hollywood pode ser genuína, principalmente quando se veem tantas versões ganharem destaque. Só em 2026, vimos Resident Evil, Street Fighter e Mortal Kombat II nas telonas.
O valor cobrado pela companhia é visto como “barato”, já que a Amazon pagou US$ 250 milhões em 2017 apenas para ter o direito de fazer uma série de O Senhor dos Anéis. Vale lembrar que o Red Dead Redemption 2 (2018) é um sucesso estrondoso, com 85 milhões de jogadores — o 3º mais vendido da história.
De acordo com o vazamento, ela busca opções nos cinemas e em séries televisivas. Na prática, não há um formato “fechado”, e o estúdio norte-americano apenas quer ver as histórias de Arthur Morgan e John Marston ganharem vida de algum modo.
Apesar do impacto de GTA 6, a Rockstar tenta vender apenas a ideia para Red Dead Redemption. Isso centraliza as decisões em torno de Grand Theft Auto dentro da desenvolvedora, assim como não prende seus personagens ou histórias ao que ocorre em filmes ou seriados.
Red Dead Redemption segue a indústria
O que o estúdio busca é o mesmo patamar que já foi consolidado por produções como The Last of Us e Fallout. Ambas as franquias transitaram bem para outra mídia, o que justifica o súbito interesse em levar uma de suas narrativas a formatos diferentes.
Por falar em séries, os próximos anos serão recheados de adaptações: Tomb Raider e God of War, por exemplo, estão nas mãos da Amazon. Far Cry também será transportado para as telas pela FX.
Nos cinemas, uma versão de Red Dead Redemption pode disputar espaço com Call of Duty, The Legend of Zelda e as sequências de Sonic the Hedgehog e Um Filme Minecraft. Porém, a desenvolvedora precisa primeiro encontrar um aliado entre os grandes estúdios de Hollywood.
Além disso, apesar do teor violento que a franquia possui, ela passa mais livremente do que outras marcas com as quais trabalha — como o próprio GTA e até Bully, que poderia render toda a revolta dos anos 2000 de volta (algo que a Rockstar tentará evitar).
